topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: End-of-life care for people with a learning disability
blurb: Recognise dying and distress in people who cannot report symptoms, talk about illness and death accessibly, and support grief and bereavement.
question: Gwen, 58, has a severe learning disability and advanced cancer. She cannot describe pain. Her support staff say she usually hums and rocks gently when content, but today she is grimacing, pulling at her blanket and has stopped humming. How should the nurse assess and respond?

teach.body: People with a learning disability have the same right as anyone to good end-of-life care: to know about their illness in a way they can understand, to be involved in decisions, to have symptoms controlled and to die where they would choose if possible. The challenges are recognising dying and distress when the person cannot report symptoms, avoiding diagnostic overshadowing, and communicating accessibly. In plain English: the Five Priorities for Care apply in full; the adjustments make them possible.
teach.cite: Five Priorities for Care (2014); NICE NG31

steps.label: Involve the person
steps.sub: In decisions, to the extent they wish

teach.body: The Disability Distress Assessment Tool (DisDAT) records how a person looks and behaves when content and when distressed: face, eyes, skin, vocal sounds, habits and mannerisms, and posture. It is completed by people who know the person well and becomes a baseline. It is not a scoring tool and does not say what is causing distress; it tells staff that the person is distressed so they can look for the cause. NICE NG31 also advises a validated behavioural pain tool for people who cannot report pain.
teach.cite: DisDAT (NTW NHS Trust, St Oswald's Hospice); NICE NG31 1.5.14

teach.caption: Distress cues are individual: one person's distress sign can be another's contentment.

teach.h: Distress at end of life: look for the cause
teach.caption: NG31 asks staff to consider urinary retention and constipation as causes of agitation in the last days of life.

teach.body: Gwen's DisDAT shows her content cues have gone and distress cues are present. The nurse does not assume this is 'behaviour' or 'part of her learning disability'. She checks for pain, a full bladder, constipation, mouth care and position, finds her abdomen tender, and contacts the palliative care team for a symptom review and anticipatory medicines. She records Gwen's response, involves her keyworker, and keeps Gwen's favourite music playing, a familiar source of comfort.

teach.text: Diagnostic overshadowing at the end of life: assuming withdrawal, agitation or not eating is part of the learning disability, or that the person 'would not understand' so need not be told. Also, signs of dying (more sleep, reduced intake, breathing changes) can also mean a reversible problem such as infection: recognise possible dying, but assess and seek experienced advice when uncertain.

teach.body: Use clear, concrete words such as 'ill', 'dying' and 'died', with pictures, photos or easy read, and repeat over time. Euphemisms like 'gone to sleep' or 'lost' can confuse or frighten. Involve people who know how the person communicates. Many people with a learning disability can understand far more than others assume, and have the right to information about their own health. If a person does not want detailed information, respect that too.

head: What you may see
How to support
rows: Name the loss; do not treat as 'behaviour'
teach.caption: Grief may show through behaviour rather than words. People should be offered the choice to take part in saying goodbye.

items: The Five Priorities for Care apply fully to people with a learning disability.
DisDAT records content and distress cues as a baseline; it is not a score.
Look for causes of distress: pain, bladder, bowels, position, mouth, fear.
Talk about illness and death in clear, concrete words with accessible formats.
Grief often shows as behaviour change; include people in goodbyes and rituals.

summary: You can now recognise distress and possible dying in people who cannot report symptoms, using DisDAT and the knowledge of those close to them. You can communicate about illness and death accessibly and support people with a learning disability through grief and bereavement.

A.q: Gwen, 58, has a severe learning disability and advanced cancer and cannot describe pain. Her staff know her well. Which tool would best help them record her usual signs of contentment and distress?
options: The Abbey pain scale for dementia
The Glasgow Coma Scale
The Disability Distress Assessment Tool
A numerical pain rating scale from 0 to 10
A.why: DisDAT records a person's usual content and distress cues (face, eyes, skin, sounds, habits, posture) to create a baseline for people with limited communication.

whyNot.0: Abbey was developed for people with dementia; DisDAT is designed for people with severe communication difficulties.
whyNot.3: Numerical scales need the person to self-report.

A.q: A healthcare assistant asks how DisDAT works. Which statement is accurate?
options: It produces a score that sets the dose of pain relief
It records the person's content and distress cues
It is completed once by the doctor on admission
It identifies the exact cause of the person's distress
A.why: DisDAT documents content and distress cues as a baseline to recognise distress; it is not a scoring tool and does not identify the cause.

whyNot.0: DisDAT is not a scoring tool.
whyNot.2: It is completed by people who know the person well and reviewed over time.
whyNot.3: It shows that distress is present; staff then look for the cause.

A.q: Shona, 35, has a moderate learning disability. Her friend at the day centre has died. Staff want to explain this to her. Which approach is best?
options: Use clear words such as 'died' with pictures
Say her friend has gone to sleep and will not wake
Wait for Shona to ask before telling her
Say her friend has moved to live somewhere else
A.why: Clear, concrete language ('died', 'dead') with pictures or easy read is easier to understand than euphemisms and respects her right to know.

whyNot.1: 'Gone to sleep' can cause confusion and fear of sleeping.
whyNot.2: Waiting can leave her confused and excluded from grieving.
whyNot.3: A false explanation can lead to waiting for the friend to return.

B.q: Ahmed, 45, has a learning disability. His mother died last month. Staff report he has become withdrawn, is eating less and is waking at night. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A new psychotic illness developing in midlife
A side effect of his regular medicines
Boredom since his routine has changed
Grief expressed through behaviour change
B.why: People with a learning disability grieve, and grief may show through behaviour change (withdrawal, appetite and sleep changes) rather than words. Physical causes should still be considered.

whyNot.1: No medicine change is described; the timing points to bereavement.
whyNot.2: Calling it boredom overlooks a major loss.

B.q: Sarah, 40, has a learning disability. Her father is dying in a hospice. Staff in her supported living home think it would be 'kinder' not to tell her or take her to the funeral. What should the nurse advise?
options: Agree, to protect Sarah from upsetting events
Tell her gently after the funeral has already taken place
Support Sarah to choose whether to visit and attend
Let her family decide without involving Sarah
B.why: Including people with a learning disability in saying goodbye and in rituals such as funerals supports healthy grieving. Sarah should be given accessible information and support to make her own choices.

whyNot.0: Exclusion denies her the chance to say goodbye and can complicate grief.
whyNot.1: Telling her afterwards removes her choice to attend.
whyNot.3: Sarah is presumed to have capacity to decide about visiting and attending.

B.q: Dora, 54, has a learning disability and terminal cancer. Using pictures, she has said she wants to die in her own home. Her staff team feel anxious about this. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Plan with the palliative care team to support her at home
Arrange a hospice bed because the staff feel unprepared for this
Tell Dora that home is not possible with her condition
Wait until she is dying and then decide where she goes
B.why: Preferred place of death should be respected where possible. Reasonable adjustments include staff training, district nursing and specialist palliative care in-reach and anticipatory medicines.

whyNot.1: Staff anxiety is a training need, not a reason to override her wish.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests home is impossible; planning makes it achievable.
whyNot.3: Leaving it late risks an unplanned admission against her wishes.

C.q: Lionel, 66, has a profound learning disability and is in the last days of life. He is grimacing and moaning, which his DisDAT lists as distress cues. A staff member says, 'He's always noisy.' What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure staff that noise is common near death
Move him to a side room so others are not disturbed
Assess for the cause and seek a symptom review
Record the behaviour and recheck in four hours
C.why: His documented distress cues suggest uncontrolled symptoms. The nurse assesses possible causes (pain, position, full bladder, constipation, mouth care) and seeks a palliative symptom review.

whyNot.0: Assuming it is normal overshadows treatable distress.
whyNot.1: Moving him addresses others' comfort, not his.
whyNot.3: Delaying assessment leaves him in distress.

C.q: Phil, 49, has Down syndrome and dementia. Over two days he has been sleeping most of the time, barely drinking and his breathing pattern has changed. What should the nurse recognise?
options: That this is typical of advanced dementia and needs no change
That he may be dying and needs urgent assessment
That he should be given fluids by mouth every hour
That his family should be told once he has died
C.why: Increased sleep, reduced intake and breathing changes may indicate the last days of life, or a reversible cause such as infection. Recognising possible dying triggers assessment, communication with family and an individual care plan.

whyNot.0: Assuming change is 'just dementia' risks missing reversible illness or dying.
whyNot.2: Forcing fluids may be unsafe and does not assess the change.
whyNot.3: Families should be told when dying is recognised so they can be involved.

C.q: Robert, 62, has a moderate learning disability and terminal heart failure. His brother asks staff not to tell Robert because 'he would not understand and it would upset him'. What should the nurse do?
options: Agree to the brother's request as his next of kin
Tell Robert the full details in medical language
Ask the consultant to decide without Robert present
Support Robert to understand in an accessible way
C.why: Robert has the same right as others to information about his health and to be involved in decisions (NG31 1.2.3: discuss prognosis unless the person does not wish to). Information is given accessibly, at his pace, with his brother's support.

whyNot.0: Next of kin cannot decide to withhold information from an adult with capacity.
whyNot.1: Medical jargon is not accessible and does not meet his communication needs.
whyNot.2: Excluding Robert breaches his right to be involved.

reteach.title: Know the person, then notice the change
reteach.question: How can you tell someone is in pain if they have never been able to tell anyone?

blocks.body: Those who know the person describe what they look and sound like when content and when distressed. When content cues disappear and distress cues appear, the person is telling you something is wrong. Your job is to find out what: pain, a full bladder, constipation, position, a dry mouth, fear.

blocks.text: DisDAT tells you distress is present. It does not tell you why, and it does not give a score.

explain.body: Signs that may suggest dying include deteriorating consciousness, agitation, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, mottled skin, noisy secretions and progressive weight loss. Some changes may be reversible; seek experienced advice when uncertain.

test.q: Which group of signs may suggest a person is in the last days of life?
options: Increased appetite and restlessness at night
Rising alertness and more conversation
Reduced consciousness and mottled skin
New interest in activities and visitors
test.why: NG31 lists signs including deteriorating consciousness, mottled skin, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, agitation and noisy secretions.

whyNot.0: Increased appetite is not a sign of dying.
whyNot.1: Rising alertness is not a sign of dying.
whyNot.3: Increased interest is not a sign of dying.

explain.body: Pain, full bladder (urinary retention), constipation, position, dry mouth, breathlessness, fear and unfamiliar surroundings. NG31 asks staff to consider retention and a full rectum in agitation.

test.q: A dying man with a profound learning disability becomes restless. Which cause should be checked as well as pain?
options: A full bladder or rectum
Low blood glucose
An allergy to the new bedding
Raised blood pressure
test.why: NG31 identifies urinary retention and a full rectum as causes of agitation in the last days of life.

whyNot.1: Routine glucose testing is not the priority check at the end of life.
whyNot.2: Bedding allergy is not a recognised common cause.
whyNot.3: Blood pressure is not a cause of restlessness to check here.

explain.body: Clear words ('dying', 'died'), pictures and easy read, repeated over time, with people who know the person's communication. Respect a wish not to know details.

test.q: Which phrase is clearest when telling a person with a learning disability that someone has died?
options: 'We have lost her'
'She has passed away'
'She has gone to sleep'
'She has died'
test.why: Concrete language such as 'died' avoids the confusion that euphemisms can cause.

whyNot.0: 'Lost' may suggest she can be found.
whyNot.1: 'Passed away' is abstract and may not be understood.
whyNot.2: 'Gone to sleep' can cause fear of sleeping and confusion.

explain.body: Grief may appear as withdrawal, agitation, sleep and appetite change or repeated questions. Offer the choice to take part in goodbyes and rituals, keep routines and familiar people, and rule out physical illness.

test.q: How might grief show in a person with a learning disability who has little speech?
options: Grief does not affect people with severe disabilities
Through changes in behaviour, sleep or appetite
Through a sudden improvement in daily skills
Through new physical symptoms of infection
test.why: Grief often appears as behaviour change: withdrawal, agitation, and sleep and appetite changes.

whyNot.0: People with severe disabilities grieve too.
whyNot.2: Grief does not typically improve skills.
whyNot.3: Infection signs should be investigated, not assumed to be grief.
